query: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited from 15–45 μm feedstock does not attain the required coating thickness. For thermal-spray deposition and subsequent service as a bond coat in a thermal barrier coating system, what single intervention could overcome this thickness shortfall while preserving coating integrity and minimal as-sprayed oxidation? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, the operating and service conditions under which it should remain effective, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment with a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Broadening the feedstock particle size distribution to include a coarser fraction (e.g., extending the upper limit from 45 μm to about 75 μm) will increase the deposited mass per pass, thereby achieving the required coating thickness while preserving coating integrity and maintaining minimal as-sprayed oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: An FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy-alloy bond coat deposited using a 15–45 μm powder feedstock that produces a coating with inadequate thickness.
generation.intervention: Modify the powder feedstock to a broader size distribution by including a coarser fraction (e.g., 15–75 μm) while keeping all other spray parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Thermal-spray deposition in a conventional setup similar to current practices; subsequent operation as a bond coat within a thermal barrier coating system under aero-engine high-temperature cyclic conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The increased mass and momentum of the coarser particles yield thicker splats during deposition, promoting enhanced layer build-up and improved inter-splat bonding, while their lower specific surface area limits additional oxidation.
generation.mechanism: Coarser particles deliver a higher mass per particle, leading to enhanced deposition efficiency. They impact with greater momentum, allowing for larger splat formation that accumulates to a sufficient coating thickness. Simultaneously, their lower surface-to-volume ratio reduces susceptibility to in-flight oxidation despite high thermal input.
generation.predicted_outcome: The coating deposited with the broadened, coarser-inclusive feedstock is expected to achieve a significantly higher thickness—meeting the required specifications—without a detrimental increase in oxidation or a loss in adhesion/integrity relative to the baseline produced from 15–45 μm feedstock.
generation.baseline: Current coatings made from 15–45 μm feedstock that fall short in thickness but exhibit minimal oxidation and acceptable integrity.
generation.boundary: This approach will be effective provided that the coarser particles do not lead to poor splat flattening or excessive in-flight deceleration; the spray parameters must remain optimized to avoid splat nonuniformity and potential defects.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative improvement in thickness and the precise limits for the coarser particle fraction remain uncertain and may require further optimization to balance deposition yield with process stability and oxidation control.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of coatings under identical thermal-spray conditions. One set uses the standard 15–45 μm feedstock (control) and the other uses the broadened feedstock with a coarser fraction (15–75 μm). All other processing parameters should remain constant. After deposition, subject both sets to the same post-deposition treatment and evaluate their microstructures, oxidation levels, and thickness.
measurements: Coating thickness via cross-sectional optical/SEM microscopy
Phase composition analysis (e.g., XRD, EDS) to assess oxidation levels
Mechanical integrity tests (e.g., adhesion/bond strength assessments)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis is falsified if the broadened feedstock does not produce a statistically significant increase in coating thickness (i.e., fails to meet the defined required thickness) or if it results in increased oxidation or compromised coating integrity compared to the standard 15–45 μm baseline.

Cold-sprayed AlFeNiCoCr alloy retains the same BCC structure as was observed in the powder []. In contrast, in the plasma-sprayed coating of the same composition, the FCC phase is observed as the major one []. Figure 8 shows the surface morphology of the APS AlCoCrFeNiSi HEA coating. From Figure 8a, it can be seen that the coating showed a rough morphology, which is usually observed on the surfaces of atmospheric plasma sprayed coatings []. It can be observed that at a higher magnification (Figure 8b), most of the splats were fully molten and well flattened, and the outlines of the flattened splats could be observed obviously. Some spherical and droplet-shaped particles with dimensions of less than 10 μm could also be found on the coating surface, which originated from the sputtering of the flying particles when impacting the already formed coating surface.
